lines.text: Two unrelated counters, one touched by each of two cores, happen to share one real cache line.
Does writing one counter ever cost the other core anything?

tolerated.line: Two unrelated counters, one touched by each of two cores, happen to share one real cache line.

lines.text: Yes, genuinely.
Every write can invalidate the other core's own cached copy.
Run it for real: the shared layout genuinely pays a real invalidation cost on every single alternating write between the two cores, even though the two counters are otherwise unrelated.

tolerated.line: Run it for real: the shared layout genuinely pays a real invalidation cost on every single alternating write between the two cores, even though the two counters are otherwise unrelated.

lines.text: Now pad each counter onto its own real cache line instead.
Does that genuinely remove the cost, or only reduce it?

tolerated.line: Now pad each counter onto its own real cache line instead.

lines.text: It genuinely removes it.
Entirely, down to zero.
Run it for real: the padded layout genuinely avoids every real cross-core invalidation, at the identical sequence of writes the shared layout paid for.

tolerated.line: Run it for real: the padded layout genuinely avoids every real cross-core invalidation, at the identical sequence of writes the shared layout paid for.

lines.text: Run both layouts again, but with far more operations this time.
Does the shared layout's own real cost grow, or does it stay the same no matter how much work runs?
Yes, it genuinely grows.
With every single additional operation.
Run it for real: the shared layout's own real cost genuinely grows with more operations, while the padded layout's own real cost stays genuinely at zero no matter how many run.
Two real, independent sources on this exact mechanism agree, in their own words.
Updating one piece of data invalidates the whole real cache line it belongs to, and padding is the real, standard fix.

So here's the real reason this cost is so easy to miss: nothing about these two counters looks wrong in the source code, since neither thread ever touches the other's variable, and that is exactly what makes the bug invisible to a correctness reviewer.

The hardware, not the program, is the one deciding the real unit of sharing, and it moves data in whole cache lines, so two values a programmer considers completely separate can still be glued together the moment the allocator happens to place them close enough.

That also closes this whole chapter's own real argument: a program's own cost can hide in a statistic nobody looked at, in a function nobody suspected, or simply in where two unrelated bytes happened to land, and all three need the identical discipline of measuring instead of assuming.
